ideas: A real deadline that forced you to learn something new
Your learning method: focus, build early, ask the right people
The result and the method you'd reuse at a customer

phrases.meaning: from the very beginning, with no previous knowledge
learn through practice, not only reading

learn.explain: FDEs constantly land in unfamiliar territory: a new customer's industry, a technology they've never used, a strange legacy system. So this question tests your learning method, not just your intelligence. A strong answer has a real time pressure, a specific skill you didn't have, and, most importantly, how you learned: what you focused on first, how you practised, who you asked, and how you checked you were right. End with a result and the method you'd use again. Show that you learn by building something small quickly, rather than reading everything first.
points: A real deadline and a clear gap in your knowledge.
A repeatable method: focus on essentials, build early, ask experts, verify.
A result, plus how you'd apply the same method at a customer.
mistakes: "I watched YouTube tutorials" with no strategy.
Choosing something too easy, with no real pressure.
Forgetting to say how you checked your understanding was correct.

betterWays.strong: My approach is to build something small on day one, even if it's ugly, and learn from what breaks.
betterWays.why: Shows a method instead of a claim.

betterWays.strong: I skipped most of the documentation and focused on the 20 percent I needed for the feature.

betterWays.weak: I didn't know nothing about it.
betterWays.strong: I had never used it before; I was starting from scratch.
betterWays.why: Fixes the double negative, sounds natural.

betterWays.strong: I asked a senior engineer for thirty minutes to review my plan before I wrote much code.
betterWays.why: Specific and shows respect for others' time.

betterWays.strong: In the end, I shipped the feature on time, and it's still running in production.

model: The situation was in the second month of my internship. The team needed a map view in the operations dashboard, showing live driver locations, and the engineer who knew the mapping library had just left. I had never used it, or worked with location data at all, and the deadline was two weeks away. So I was really starting from scratch. What I did was, first, not try to learn everything. I wrote down the three things the feature actually needed: show points on a map, update them every few seconds, and group them when zoomed out. That was the 20 percent that matters. Then I learned by doing: on day one I built a tiny, ugly version with fake data, just to see what broke. On day three, I booked thirty minutes with a senior engineer to review my plan, and she warned me about a performance problem with thousands of points that would have cost me days. Finally, I tested it with the real operators before the deadline, not after. As a result, I got up to speed in about a week, shipped on time, and the map is still in use. It's the same approach I'd use at a new customer: find what matters, build early, and ask the right person early.
short: In my internship, I had two weeks to build a live map feature with a library I'd never used. What I did was list the three things the feature really needed, build an ugly version on day one, and get a thirty-minute review from a senior engineer, which saved me days. As a result, I shipped on time. I'd use the same approach at a new customer.

followUps.q: How do you know when you understand something well enough?
followUps.answer: When I can explain it simply to someone else and predict what will happen before I run it. If my predictions are often wrong, I don't understand it yet, even if the code works.

followUps.q: What are you learning right now?
followUps.answer: Two things: how to build reliable AI systems, especially testing them properly, and spoken English for technical conversations. For both, I practise with real tasks every day rather than only reading.

followUps.q: What if there's no senior engineer to ask?
followUps.answer: Then I look for other sources of truth: the official documentation for the specific problem, the source code, or the people who use the system every day. At a customer, their own staff often know things no document says.

selfCheck: There was a real deadline and a real knowledge gap.
